newsitem.title: USA: Ideas, not deals seen in U.S.-Asia services talks.
newsitem.headline: Ideas, not deals seen in U.S.-Asia services talks.

text.p: Talks next week between top American and Asian officials on liberalizing financial services will lay down broad objectives rather than bring concrete deals, according to a senior Treasury official.

"We are not trying to negotiate anything specific on this trip, we are going to lay down broad objectives and an extensive set of proposals for how we are going to accommodate their concerns," said the official, who asked not to be named.
"We do not expect ... to conclude the trip with any announcements of concrete deals. This is the first stage of the process."

A U.S. delegation led by Deputy Trade Representative Jeffrey Lang and Senior Deputy Assistant Treasury Secretary Timothy Geithner is due to start an Asia trip on Monday with discussions in Tokyo on the status of World Trade Organization talks to open up financial services markets.

The officials will then visit other Asian states, including Thailand, the Philippines and Indonesia -- all of which are recovering from turmoil on domestic financial markets and the shock of forced currency devaluations.

"What we are going to do is try to send a signal to these countries that this (financial services liberalization) is important to the United States, that we want a successful agreement," the Treasury official said.
"We think everyone needs to look through the current (currency) crisis and ... work to the types of things that will be critical to a long-term solution."
The United States has been one of the strongest proponents of a global deal to liberalize financial markets, which would make it easier for U.S. banks and insurance firms to do business abroad.

Other countries, especially in the developing world, have argued that giving foreign firms access to their markets could hurt domestic banks or threaten their own security by boosting access to fickle speculative capital.
But the Treasury official said many officials in Asia recognized the advantages of liberalized financial markets.

"Most people recognise that financial liberalization is a critical part of that (long-term solution), both because they need to attract the capital to finance growth over time and because they need to attract foreign capital and strengthen their banking systems," he said.
The Treasury official said efforts to boost financial stability in Asia would also be on the agenda during the trip.

"We have a major stake in seeing financial stability restored in Asia," he said. "We are involved in a whole range of initiatives ... to help strengthen financial systems in emerging markets and we are going to be talking about that set of initiatives on this trip and over the next several weeks."
